## 1. Overview

This hands-on exercise demonstrates the practical application of
**geospatial predictive modelling** using the **geographical random
forest (GRF)** method. It builds on the key principle that spatial
events are neither randomly nor uniformly distributed, guiding you to
explore how historical geospatial occurrences can be linked with
environmental variables that reflect spatial constraints and influences.

The workflow involves preparing training and test datasets through
appropriate spatial sampling techniques, calibrating predictive models
using both **geospatial statistical learning** and **machine learning**
approaches, and performing model comparison and selection to identify
the best predictive model. Finally, the chosen model is used to generate
future outcome predictions. Together, these steps illustrate how known
spatial patterns and predictor variables can be leveraged to forecast
future events within a geospatial framework.

### 2. Learning Outcomes

In this hands-on exercise, predictive modelling will be implemented by
using the geographical random forest method.

The process involves:

-   preparing training and test data sets by using appropriate data
    sampling methods;

-   calibrating predictive models by using geospatial statistical
    learning and machine learning methods;

-   comparing and selecting the best model for predicting the future
    outcome;

-   predicting the future outcomes by using the best calibrated model.

## 3. The Data

The study integrates both **aspatial** and **geospatial** datasets to
model HDB resale prices in Singapore from Jan 2017 onwards.

| Dataset | Description | Format |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Aspatial dataset | HDB Resale data: a list of HDB resale transacted prices in Singapore from Jan 2017 onwards, downloaded from [Data.gov.sg.](Data.gov.sg) | CSV |
| Geospatial dataset | *P14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL*: a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2014 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data, also downloaded from [Data.gov.sg.](Data.gov.sg) | ESRI shapefile |
| Locational factors with geographic coordinates | Eldercare centres, Hawker centres ,Parks ,Supermarkets ,CHAS clinics ,Childcare services ,Kindergartens downloaded from [Data.gov.sg](Data.gov.sg) MRT/LRT stations ,Bus stops downloaded from [Datamall.lta.gov.sg](Datamall.lta.gov.sg), | GeoJSON or Shapefile |
| Locational factors without geographic coordinates | Primary schools, extracted from Data.gov.sg’s school information dataset. CBD coordinates, retrieved from Google. Shopping malls , scraped from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_shopping_malls_in_Singapore). Good primary schools , ranked list of popular schools from[Local Salary Forum.](https://www.salary.sg/2021/best-primary-schools-2021-by-popularity/) | CSV |

{tbl-colwidths="\[30,60,10\]"}

## 4. Installing and Loading R packages

Following packages are being used here,

| Name | Description |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| [GWmodel](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GWmodel/index.html) | Calibrates geographical weighted family of models |
| [rsample](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/) | Provides functions to create different types of resamples and corresponding classes for their analysis. |
| [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/) | Handles importing, managing, and processing vector-based geospatial data |
| [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) | A collection of R packages for data wrangling and visualisation, including **readr**, **dplyr**, and **ggplot2**. |
| [tmap](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/) | Creates cartographic quality static and interactive thematic (choropleth) maps. |
| [SpatialML](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/SpatialML/index.html) | Allows for a geographically weighted random forest regression including a function to find the optical bandwidth.  |
| [Metrics](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Metrics/index.html) | Implements metrics for regression, time series, binary classification, classification, and information retrieval problems. |
| [spdep](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/spdep/index.html) | Provides tools for spatial dependence: building neighbour lists, spatial weights, and spatial autocorrelation analysis. |

{tbl-colwidths="\[15,85\]"}

We load the following packages into R environment.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, GWmodel, SpatialML, 
               tmap, rsample, Metrics, tidyverse)
```
:::



## 5. Preparing Data

### 5.a. Reading data file to rds

We first read the input data sets that is saved in `simple feature` data
frame.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mdata <- read_rds("data/rawdata/mdata.rds")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glimpse(mdata)
```
:::



### 5.b. Data Sampling

We split the entire data into 65% training and 35% test by using
`initial_split()` of **rsample** package, which belongs to
**tigymodels** ecosystem.

Later we extract the training set and test set from a data split object
created by functions `initial_split()`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1234)
resale_split <- initial_split(mdata, prop = 6.5/10,)
train_data <- training(resale_split)
test_data <- testing(resale_split)
```
:::



We save both files.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(train_data, "data/model/train_data.rds")
write_rds(test_data, "data/model/test_data.rds")
```
:::



### 5.c. Computing Correlation Matrix

Before loading predictors into a predictive model, let's plot the
correlation matrix to check if there is any sign of multicolinearity



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mdata_nogeo <- st_drop_geometry(mdata)
corrplot::corrplot(cor(mdata_nogeo[, 2:17]),
                   diag = FALSE, # hide diagonal or TRUE
                   order = "AOE",# angular order of the eigenvectors" /original/AOE/FPC/hclust/alphabet
                   tl.pos = "td", # text label position: top and diagonal/lt/n null
                   tl.cex = 0.5,  # text label size: shrinks 50%
                   method = "number",  # display number/circle/color/shade/pie
                   type = "upper") #show only the upper triangle/full/lower
```
:::



There is no sign of multicolinearity since all correlation values are
below **0.8**.

## 6. Retriving the Stored Data

We load the saved data into R.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_data <- read_rds("data/model/train_data.rds")
test_data <- read_rds("data/model/test_data.rds")
```
:::



## 7. Building a Non-spatial Multiple Linear Regression

A multiple regression model is built as a base line model.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
price_mlr <- lm(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +                   
                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                  PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
                  PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                  WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                  WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                data=train_data)
summary(price_mlr)
```
:::



This linear regression model shows a strong explanatory power,
accounting for about **73.7% of the variation in HDB resale prices**.
The key determinants include **structural factors** such as floor area
(adding roughly **\$2,781 per sqm**) and storey height (adding about
**\$14,299 per level**). **Locational attributes** also play a major
role — proximity to **MRT stations, the CBD, and hawker centres**
notably increases resale values. Overall, the model highlights that both
**physical characteristics** and **accessibility to amenities** are
critical in shaping HDB resale prices across Singapore.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(price_mlr, "data/model/price_mlr.rds" ) 
```
:::



## 8. gwr Predictive Method

We now build and calibrate geographically weighted regression model to
predict the HDB resales prices using methods from
[GWmodel](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GWmodel/index.html)
package.

C`omputing Predicted Values of the Test Data` suggests that we need to
convert the data to spatial objects first. Convert the training and test
data into `SpatialPointDateFrame` for use in GWR:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_data_sp <- as(train_data, "Spatial")
test_data_sp <- as(test_data, "Spatial")
train_data_sp
test_data_sp
```
:::



### 8.a. Computing Adaptive Bandwidth

We use the `bw.gwr()` function from the **GWmodel** package to determine
the optimal bandwidth. The “CV” (Cross Validation) method is chosen for
calibration because, between the two available options “CV” and “AIC”,
the CV method generally produces a smaller bandwidth, allowing the model
to capture more local variation in the data.

The code chunk below computes and saves the optimal bandwidth. The
search can be time consuming and computationally intensive.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  approach="CV",
  kernel="gaussian",
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat=FALSE)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(bw_adaptive, "data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")
```
:::



We've found optimal bandwidth is 40 neighour points.

### 8.b. Constructing the Adaptive Bandwidth GWR Model

Let us call the save bandwidth by using the code chunk below.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bw_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bw_adaptive
```
:::



Then we build the GWR-based hedonic pricing model using adaptive
bandwidth and Gaussian kernel. Same reason as the previous step, we save
a copy of the `gwrm` file.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwr_adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_sp,
  bw=bw_adaptive, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
write_rds(gwr_adaptive, 
          "data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")
```
:::



### 8.c. Retrieve gwr Output Object

We re-load the saved `gwrm` object and retrieve the report of model
output.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwr_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwr_adaptive
```
:::



The report reads that R2 value has increased from 0.7373 to 0.9677
indicating model's fit has substantially proved and information loss has
decreased as AICc down from 257320.3 to 238871.8.

### 8.d. Computing Adaptive Bandwidth for the Test Data



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=test_data_sp,
  approach="CV", #   note we use approach="CV" compared with bw=bw_adaptive in training
  kernel="gaussian",
  adaptive=TRUE,
  longlat=FALSE)

write_rds(gwr_bw_test_adaptive, 
          "data/model/gwr_bw_test_adaptive.rds")
```
:::



The Cross-validation determines the optimal adaptive bandwidth is **25**
for the test set.

### 8.e. Computing Predicted Values of the Test Data



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwr_pred <- gwr.predict(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + 
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + 
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + 
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, 
  data=train_data, 
  predictdata = test_data, 
  bw=40, 
  kernel = 'gaussian', 
  adaptive=TRUE, 
  longlat = FALSE)

write_rds(gwr_pred, 
          "data/model/gwr_pred.rds")
```
:::



## 9. Calibrating Random Forest Model

Now, we calibrate the model by using random forest function from
[ranger](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html)
package.

### 9.a. Preparing Coordinates Data

First we calculate x,y coordinates matrix for whole dataset, and
training and test sets.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_data <- read_rds("data/model/train_data.rds")
test_data <- read_rds("data/model/test_data.rds")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coords <- st_coordinates(mdata)
coords_train <- st_coordinates(train_data)
coords_test <- st_coordinates(test_data)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coords_train <- write_rds(coords_train, "data/geospatial/coords_train.rds" )
coords_test <- write_rds(coords_test, "data/geospatial/coords_test.rds" )
```
:::



### 9.b. Dropping Geometry Field

The geometry column should be removed since it is not required for the
upcoming analysis. The code chunk below uses `st_drop_geometry()`
function from the **sf** package to drop the `geometry`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_data_nogeom <- train_data %>% st_drop_geometry()
test_data_nogeom <- test_data %>% st_drop_geometry()
```
:::



### 9.c. Calibrating a Non-spatial Random Forest Model



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1234)
rf <- ranger(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + 
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS +  
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data=train_data_nogeom)

rf
```
:::



The Ranger result shows our R2 value is 0.9496 that is much higher than
non-spatial regression model.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(rf, "data/model/rf.rds")
```
:::



## 10. Calibrating Geographical Weighted Random Forest Model

Next we `grf()` of
[SpatialML](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html)
package to calibrate a geographic random forest model.

### 10.a. Calibrating Using Training Data

We apply `grf()` of
[SpatialML](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html)
package to calibrate model on training data.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1234)
gwRF_adaptive <- grf(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + 
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + 
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + 
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + 
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  dframe=train_data_nogeom, 
  bw=40,
  kernel="adaptive",
  coords=coords_train)
```
:::



R2 on the training set is 0.9515.

We again save the new model on training data.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write_rds(gwRF_adaptive, "data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")
```
:::



Then we retrieve the model for next steps.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwRF_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")
```
:::



### 10.b. Predicting by using Test Data

#### 10.b.1. Preparing the Test Data

Now we use `cbind()` to combine `test_data` and `coords_test` and remove
the `geometry`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
test_data_nogeom <- cbind(test_data, coords_test)%>%
  st_drop_geometry()
```
:::



#### 10.b.2. Predicting with Test Data

Next, We use `predict.grf()` of **SpatialML** package to predict the
resale price using `gwPF_adaptive` model on the test data.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gwRF_pred <- predict.grf(gwRF_adaptive, 
                        test_data_nogeom, 
                        x.var.name="X",
                        y.var.name="Y", 
                        local.w=1,
                        global.w=0)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
GRF_pred <- write_rds(gwRF_pred, "data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
```
:::



#### 10.b.3. Converting the Predicting Output into a data.frame

We reload the saved predicting output (generated from `predict.grf()` in
the previous step) back to R and convert it into a data frame for
further study since the original output is in `numeric` format.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
GRF_pred_df <- as.data.frame(GRF_pred)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glimpse(GRF_pred_df)
```
:::



To compare the actual and predicted, we combine the with `GRF_pred_df`
and select required columns: `resale_price`in `test_data` and `GRF_pred`
the column where predicting outputs are in `GRF_pred_df` into a new data
frame called `test_data_p` and save it on the disk.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
test_data_p <- cbind(test_data, GRF_pred_df) %>%
  select(resale_price, GRF_pred)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glimpse(test_data_p)
write_rds(test_data_p,"data/model/test_data_p.rds")
```
:::



#### 10.b.4. Calculating Root Mean Square Error

To measure the difference between actual and predicted in the regression
model, we use `rmse()` of **Metrics** package to compute the Root Mean
Square Error (RMSE). The RMSE is 28160.87 for this GWR model.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rmse(test_data_p$resale_price, test_data_p$GRF_pred)
```
:::



#### 10.b.5. Visualising the Predicted Values

Alternatively, we use **scatterplot** to visualise how far the predicted
values deviate from the actual ones using the functions `geom_point()`
and `ggplot()`.

For the reference line, we use `geom_abline()` to create a 45-degree
line in the positive quadrant by setting the arguments `slope = 1` and
`intercept = 0`. To customise the line style, we can specify the
`linetype` argument using numeric values or their names: 0: blank 1:
solid (default) 2: dashed 3: dotted 4: dotdash 5: longdash 6: twodash



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = test_data_p, aes(x= GRF_pred, y = resale_price)) +
  geom_point() +
 geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 1, size = 0.8)
```
:::



Based on the visual analysis, the scatterplot indicates that the model
achieves strong predictive accuracy, as most data points closely align
with the 45-degree reference line. This tight clustering suggests a high
level of agreement between the predicted and actual resale prices.
Additionally, the plot shows only a few noticeable outliers, implying
that prediction errors are generally minimal and the model performs
reliably across most observations.
